records.gloss: An oracle: [the] word of Yahweh to Israel by [the] hand of Malachi.
pieces: An oracle: the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to Israel \q through Malachi.

L.1: An oracle: the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to Israel \q by the hand of Malachi.

R.1: A message: the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to Israel, \q given through Malachi.

decisions.choice: an oracle: a solemn message from God
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "lift up", and is used for a message the prophet lifts up his voice to deliver. Older translations rendered it "burden". It heads Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1 in the same way: "An oracle: the word of the LORD". |

decisions.choice: Malachi: the prophet's name, which means "my messenger"
alternatives: "my messenger", as a title rather than a name
decisions.reason: The name means "my messenger", the same word the LORD uses in 3:1 ("I am sending my messenger"). Nothing else is known of the prophet, and some think the word here is a title drawn from 3:1, not a personal name. The Greek translation is generally said to read "by the hand of his messenger", and the Aramaic Targum adds "whose name is called Ezra the scribe". The book is read here as the words of a prophet named Malachi.

decisions.choice: the time of Malachi: after the temple was rebuilt, in the Persian period
decisions.reason: The temple is standing and sacrifices are offered (1:10; 3:1, 10), and a governor rules (1:8), so the book comes from after 515 BC. Its concerns, careless priests, marriage to foreign wives, and tithes withheld, are those Ezra and Nehemiah dealt with in the middle of the fifth century BC (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 13), so it is usually dated near their time. |

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD to Israel: a series of disputes
decisions.reason: The book is built of six disputes (1:2-5; 1:6-2:9; 2:10-16; 2:17-3:5; 3:6-12; 3:13-21), each following one pattern: the LORD makes a statement, the people object, "But you say, ...?", and the LORD answers. "Israel" here is the whole people of God living in Judah after the exile. |

decisions.choice: oracle (L, B), message (R); the disputes set in lines
decisions.reason: Massa' follows the Isaiah table. Malachi is close to prose, but it is a prophet's oracle and its verses divide clearly at the Hebrew accents, so it is set in lines at every level, breaking at the main accent and, where a verse is long, at the lesser ones. The people's questions are set in double quotes and the LORD's words have none, as in Isaiah. |

records.heading: I have loved you

records.source: אָהַ֤בְתִּי אֶתְכֶם֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם בַּמָּ֣ה אֲהַבְתָּ֑נוּ הֲלוֹא־אָ֨ח עֵשָׂ֤ו לְיַֽעֲקֹב֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה וָאֹהַ֖ב אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹֽב׃
records.gloss: I have loved you, says Yahweh; and you say, In what have you loved us? [Was] not Esau a brother to Jacob? declaration of Yahweh; and I loved Jacob,
pieces: I have loved you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q Yet you ask, "In what way have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved us?" \q Was Esau not Jacob's brother? declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q Even so, I loved Jacob,

L.2: I have loved you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q But you say, "How have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved us?" \q Is not Esau a brother to Jacob? declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q And I loved Jacob,

R.2: I have loved you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q But you say, "How have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} shown us love?" \q Esau was Jacob's brother, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q Yet I chose to love Jacob,

decisions.choice: I have loved you: the LORD's covenant love, by which he chose his people
decisions.reason: The love meant here is the LORD's choice of Israel and his faithfulness to that choice. "It was not because you were more numerous than any other people that the LORD set his love on you ... but because the LORD loved you" (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). The book begins with this love before any rebuke. |

decisions.choice: But you say, "How have you loved us?": the pattern of the disputes
decisions.reason: The people answer every statement of the LORD with a question that challenges it (1:6, 7; 2:14, 17; 3:7, 8, 13). Here they doubt that he loves them at all, after years of hardship. The questions are quoted words of the people. |

decisions.choice: Esau and Jacob: the ancestors of Edom and Israel
decisions.reason: Esau and Jacob were twin sons of Isaac; Esau's descendants became the people of Edom, south-east of Judah, and Jacob's became Israel (Genesis 25:23-30; 36:1). Though they were brothers, the LORD chose Jacob, the younger. |

decisions.choice: And I loved Jacob (L), Even so, I loved Jacob (B); Yet I chose to love Jacob (R)
decisions.reason: With the first words of verse 3, the line reads "I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated" (L, B) and "I chose to love Jacob, but I rejected Esau" (R), the wording published in Romans 9:13. The LORD's question "How have you loved us?" uses the deity_pronoun setting, because the people speak to him. |

records.source: וְאֶת־עֵשָׂ֖ו שָׂנֵ֑אתִי וָאָשִׂ֤ים אֶת־הָרָיו֙ שְׁמָמָ֔ה וְאֶת־נַחֲלָת֖וֹ לְתַנּ֥וֹת מִדְבָּֽר׃
records.gloss: but Esau I hated, and I have made his mountains a desolation and his inheritance for [the] jackals of [the] wilderness.
pieces: but Esau I hated. \q I have turned his mountains into a wasteland \q and left his inheritance to the jackals of the desert.

L.3: but Esau I hated, \q and I have made his mountains a desolation \q and his inheritance [a place] for the jackals of the wilderness.

R.3: but I rejected Esau. \q I have turned his mountains into a wasteland \q and left his land to the jackals of the desert.

decisions.choice: I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated: I chose Jacob, and did not choose Esau
decisions.reason: In Hebrew, "love" and "hate" set side by side often mean preferring one and setting the other aside, not the feelings the words usually name. Jacob "loved" Rachel and "hated" Leah, meaning he loved her less (Genesis 29:30-31); Deuteronomy 21:15 speaks of a loved wife and a "hated" one. Jesus' saying that his followers must "hate" their families (Luke 14:26) is given in Matthew 10:37 as loving them "more than me". Here the LORD chose Jacob to be his people and did not choose Esau.

decisions.choice: quoted in Romans 9:13
decisions.reason: Paul quotes "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" in Romans 9:13 to show that God's choice rests on his own purpose, not on what people do. |

decisions.choice: his mountains a desolation: the ruin of Edom
decisions.reason: Edom's land was the hill country of Seir, south-east of the Dead Sea. After the fall of Jerusalem, Edom itself was overrun, by the Babylonian king Nabonidus in the 550s BC and then by Arab peoples moving in from the desert, who later became the Nabateans. By Malachi's day its towns lay in ruins. |

decisions.choice: but I rejected Esau (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "Esau I hated", and Readable says "I rejected Esau", as in Romans 9:13 at each level. The idiom decision (m1) explains the sense. |

records.source: כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֱד֜וֹם רֻשַּׁ֗שְׁנוּ וְנָשׁוּב֙ וְנִבְנֶ֣ה חֳרָב֔וֹת כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת הֵ֥מָּה יִבְנ֖וּ וַאֲנִ֣י אֶהֱר֑וֹס וְקָרְא֤וּ לָהֶם֙ גְּב֣וּל רִשְׁעָ֔ה וְהָעָ֛ם אֲשֶׁר־זָעַ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה עַד־עוֹלָֽם׃
records.gloss: Though Edom says, We have been shattered, but we will return and build [the] ruins, thus says Yahweh of hosts: They will build, but I will tear down; and they will be called [the] territory of wickedness, and the people with whom Yahweh is indignant forever.
pieces: Edom may say, "We have been crushed, but we will rebuild the ruins." \q But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: They may build, but I will tear down. \q They will be called the Land of Wickedness, \q the people with whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is angry forever.

L.4: If Edom says, "We have been shattered, but we will return and build the ruins," \q thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: They will build, but I will tear down; \q and they will be called the territory of wickedness, \q and the people with whom {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is indignant forever.

R.4: The people of Edom may say, "Our towns have been destroyed, but we will build them again." \q But this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: They can build, but I will tear it all down. \q People will call their country the Land of Evil, \q and they will be known as the people {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is always angry with.

decisions.choice: Edom's words: a boast that it will recover
decisions.reason: Edom's own words are quoted. It admits the ruin but expects to rebuild. The LORD answers that he will undo whatever it builds. |

decisions.choice: the territory of wickedness: a name that shows what they are
decisions.reason: Israel's land is called the LORD's holy land (Zechariah 2:16); Edom's will be named for its wickedness. "The people with whom the LORD is indignant" is a second such name. |

decisions.choice: indignant forever: under the LORD's lasting anger
decisions.reason: The verb means to be indignant, to denounce or curse (Numbers 23:7-8; Proverbs 24:24). Edom's fall is lasting, unlike Israel's, which the LORD reversed. |

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD of hosts (L), The LORD of Armies says this (B), This is what the LORD of Armies says (R)
decisions.reason: The formula follows the Isaiah table. Edom's words are quoted in double quotes. Balanced and Readable write "Land of Wickedness" and "Land of Evil" with capitals as a name. |

records.source: וְעֵינֵיכֶ֖ם תִּרְאֶ֑ינָה וְאַתֶּ֤ם תֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ יִגְדַּ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה מֵעַ֖ל לִגְב֥וּל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And your eyes will see, and you will say, Great [is] Yahweh beyond the border of Israel.
pieces: You will see it with your own eyes, \q and you will say, "Great is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q even beyond the borders of Israel!"

L.5: Your own eyes will see it, \q and you will say, "Great is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} \q beyond the border of Israel!"

R.5: You will see this for yourselves. \q Then you will say, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is great, \q even outside the land of Israel!"

decisions.choice: beyond the border of Israel: the LORD's greatness reaches past Israel's land
decisions.reason: The words can mean "above" or "beyond" the border. Most take them as "beyond": the LORD's rule is seen in what he does to Edom, outside Israel. Read the other way, the people praise him for what he does over Israel's own land.

decisions.choice: you will say: the doubters of verse 2 will praise
decisions.reason: Those who asked "How have you loved us?" will answer their own question when they see what happens to Edom. |

decisions.choice: the people's words in double quotes
decisions.reason: The people's words of praise are quoted, as their questions are. |

records.source: בֵּ֛ן יְכַבֵּ֥ד אָ֖ב וְעֶ֣בֶד אֲדֹנָ֑יו וְאִם־אָ֣ב אָ֣נִי אַיֵּ֣ה כְבוֹדִ֡י וְאִם־אֲדוֹנִ֣ים אָנִי֩ אַיֵּ֨ה מוֹרָאִ֜י אָמַ֣ר׀יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת לָכֶם֙ הַכֹּֽהֲנִים֙ בּוֹזֵ֣י שְׁמִ֔י וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֕ם בַּמֶּ֥ה בָזִ֖ינוּ אֶת־שְׁמֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: A son honors [his] father, and a slave his master. And if I [am] a father, where [is] my honor? And if I [am] a master, where [is] my fear? says Yahweh of hosts to you, the priests, despisers of my name. And you say, In what have we despised your name?
pieces: A son honors his father, and a servant honors his master. \q If I am a father, where is the honor due to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? If I am a master, where is the respect due to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies to you priests who despise {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. \q Yet you ask, "In what way have we despised {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name?"

L.6: A son honors [his] father, and a slave his master. \q And if a father [am] I, where [is] {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} honor? And if a master [am] I, where [is] the fear of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts to you, O priests, who despise {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. \q But you say, "How have we despised {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name?"

R.6: A son honors his father, and a servant respects his master. \q I am a father to you, so why do you not honor {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? I am your master, so why do you not respect {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies. You priests treat {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name with contempt! \q But you ask, "How have we treated {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name with contempt?"

decisions.choice: a slave and his master: a servant owned by his master
decisions.reason: The word means a servant who belonged to his master, not a hired worker. Such a servant owed his master obedience and respect, as a son owed honor to his father. The LORD is both father (2:10; Isaiah 63:16) and master to his people. |

decisions.choice: where is my fear: where is the respect owed to me
decisions.reason: "Fear" here is reverence and respect, the honor a servant owes his master. |

decisions.choice: who despise my name: who treat the LORD himself with contempt
decisions.reason: The LORD's name stands for the LORD himself, as he has made himself known (Exodus 3:15). The priests, whose task was to honor it, show contempt for it by what they offer (verses 7-8). |

decisions.choice: the priests: the dispute of 1:6-2:9 is addressed to the priests
decisions.reason: The priests served at the altar of the rebuilt temple. The LORD's charge against them runs to 2:9, where it ends with his covenant with Levi. |

decisions.choice: slave (L), servant (B, R)
decisions.reason: The word follows the style guide's rule: "slave" at Literal, "servant" at Balanced and Readable, with the servant's position stated in m1. The people's question is set in double quotes and uses the deity_pronoun setting, because they speak to the LORD. |

records.source: מַגִּישִׁ֤ים עַֽל־מִזְבְּחִי֙ לֶ֣חֶם מְגֹאָ֔ל וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם בַּמֶּ֣ה גֵֽאַלְנ֑וּךָ בֶּאֱמָרְכֶ֕ם שֻׁלְחַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה נִבְזֶ֥ה הֽוּא׃
records.gloss: [You are] presenting on my altar defiled food. And you say, In what have we defiled you? In your saying, [The] table of Yahweh, it [is] despicable.
pieces: You offer defiled food on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar. \q Yet you ask, "In what way have we defiled {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?" \q By saying, \q "The table of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} may be despised."

L.7: You are presenting defiled food on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar. \q But you say, "How have we defiled {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?" \q By your saying, \q "The table of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is despicable."

R.7: You put food on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar that is not fit to offer. \q But you ask, "How have we made {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} unclean?" \q You do it by saying, "We do not need to respect {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s altar."

decisions.choice: defiled food: offerings unfit for the altar
decisions.reason: The sacrifices are called the "food" of God (Leviticus 21:6, 8; 3:11), not because he needs to eat but because they are presented at his table. Verse 8 says what makes them defiled. |

decisions.choice: the table of the LORD: the altar
decisions.reason: Ezekiel 41:22 and 44:16 call the altar "the table that is before the LORD". The priests treat the place where the LORD is served as of no account. |

decisions.choice: How have we defiled you?: defiling the offering defiles the LORD
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "defiled you": to treat his altar with contempt is to treat the LORD himself so. The Greek translation is generally said to read "defiled it", referring to the food.

decisions.choice: the people's words in double quotes
decisions.reason: The priests did not say these words aloud; their actions say them. They are set as quoted words, as the book quotes the people throughout. Readable says "altar" for "table", the sense of m2. |

records.source: וְכִֽי־תַגִּשׁ֨וּן עִוֵּ֤ר לִזְבֹּ֨חַ֙ אֵ֣ין רָ֔ע וְכִ֥י תַגִּ֛ישׁוּ פִּסֵּ֥חַ וְחֹלֶ֖ה אֵ֣ין רָ֑ע הַקְרִיבֵ֨הוּ נָ֜א לְפֶחָתֶ֗ךָ הֲיִּרְצְךָ֙א֚וֹ הֲיִשָּׂ֣א פָנֶ֔יךָ אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And when you present a blind [one] for sacrifice, [is it] not evil? And when you present [the] lame and [the] sick, [is it] not evil? Present it, please, to your governor; will he be pleased with you or lift up your face? says Yahweh of hosts.
pieces: When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not wrong? \q When you offer animals that are lame or sick, is that not wrong? \q Just try offering such a thing to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or receive you kindly? \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

L.8: And when you present a blind [animal] for sacrifice, is it not evil? \q And when you present the lame and the sick, is it not evil? \q Present it, please, to your governor; will he be pleased with you or lift up your face? \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts.

R.8: You bring blind animals to sacrifice. Is that not wrong? \q You bring animals that are lame or sick. Is that not wrong? \q Try giving them to your governor! Would he be pleased with you? Would he accept you? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

decisions.choice: blind, lame and sick animals: animals the law forbade for sacrifice
decisions.reason: Animals for sacrifice had to be without defect: blind, lame or sick animals were not to be offered (Leviticus 22:20-25; Deuteronomy 15:21). The priests were letting people offer what they did not want themselves. |

decisions.choice: your governor: the Persian governor of Judah
decisions.reason: Judah was a province of the Persian empire, ruled by a governor, as Zerubbabel had been (Haggai 1:1) and Nehemiah later was (Nehemiah 5:14-15). People brought gifts to a governor, and no one would dare give him a sick animal. |

decisions.choice: lift up your face: receive you with favor
decisions.reason: To lift someone's face is to accept him, to grant his request (Genesis 32:21; Job 42:8). The same idiom returns in verse 9. |

decisions.choice: is it not evil?: a question
decisions.reason: The words can be read as the LORD's question or as the priests' careless claim ("It does not matter!"). Read either way, the LORD's verdict is plain.

decisions.choice: animals (B, R); wrong (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets "[animal]"; Balanced and Readable say "animals". Balanced and Readable say "wrong" for "evil", which here means a wrong done. |

records.source: וְעַתָּ֛ה חַלּוּ־נָ֥א פְנֵי־אֵ֖ל וִֽיחָנֵ֑נוּמִיֶּדְכֶם֙ הָ֣יְתָה זֹּ֔את הֲיִשָּׂ֤א מִכֶּם֙ פָּנִ֔ים אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And now, entreat, please, [the] face of God, that he may be gracious to us. From your hand this has been; will he lift up faces from you? says Yahweh of hosts.
pieces: So now, plead with God to be gracious to us! \q With such offerings from your hands, \q will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} show favor to any of you? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

L.9: And now, entreat the face of God, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may be gracious to us! \q From your hand this has come; \q will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lift up the face of any of you? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts.

R.9: So now, go ahead and ask God to be kind to us! \q But when you bring offerings like these, \q will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} accept any of you? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

decisions.choice: entreat the favor of God: seek his goodwill in prayer
decisions.reason: The phrase means "soften the face" of someone, that is, to seek favor (Exodus 32:11; 1 Kings 13:6). |

decisions.choice: a call to prayer, spoken in irony
decisions.reason: The prophet urges the priests to pray for the people ("us"), but with offerings like theirs the LORD will not hear. The question at the end expects the answer "no". |

decisions.choice: from your hand this has come: this is your doing
decisions.reason: The defective offerings came from the priests' own hands, so the LORD's refusal is their own fault. |

decisions.choice: entreat the favor (L), plead with God (B), ask God to be kind (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the picture of the face (m1). Balanced and Readable add "with such offerings" and "offerings like these" to make "this" plain. |

records.source: מִ֤י גַם־בָּכֶם֙ וְיִסְגֹּ֣ר דְּלָתַ֔יִם וְלֹֽא־תָאִ֥ירוּ מִזְבְּחִ֖י חִנָּ֑ם אֵֽין־לִ֨י חֵ֜פֶץ בָּכֶ֗ם אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת וּמִנְחָ֖ה לֹֽא־אֶרְצֶ֥ה מִיֶּדְכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Who also among you [is there] that he would shut the doors, and you would not kindle my altar in vain? I have no pleasure in you, says Yahweh of hosts, and an offering I will not accept from your hand.
pieces: If only one of you would close the temple doors \q and stop you from lighting useless fires on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar! \q I have no pleasure in you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, \q and I will not accept an offering from your hands.

L.10: Who is there even among you who would shut the doors, \q so that you would not kindle {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar in vain? \q I have no pleasure in you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, \q and an offering I will not accept from your hand.

R.10: I wish someone among you would lock the temple doors, \q so that you would stop lighting useless fires on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} altar! \q I am not pleased with you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies. \q I will not accept any offering you bring.

decisions.choice: who among you would shut the doors?: a wish
decisions.reason: A question beginning "who" can express a wish (2 Samuel 15:4; Psalm 55:7). The LORD would rather have the temple closed than receive such worship. |

decisions.choice: the doors: the gates of the temple courts
decisions.reason: The doors are those of the temple and its courts, where the altar stood. Shutting them would end the sacrifices. |

decisions.choice: offering: a gift brought to God
decisions.reason: The word is used for the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1) and for offerings in general. Here it means any gift the priests bring. |

decisions.choice: the temple doors (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say which doors are meant (m2). |

records.source: כִּ֣י מִמִּזְרַח־שֶׁ֜מֶשׁ וְעַד־מְבוֹא֗וֹ גָּד֤וֹל שְׁמִי֙ בַּגּוֹיִ֔ם וּבְכָל־מָק֗וֹם מֻקְטָ֥ר מֻגָּ֛שׁ לִשְׁמִ֖י וּמִנְחָ֣ה טְהוֹרָ֑ה כִּֽי־גָד֤וֹל שְׁמִי֙ בַּגּוֹיִ֔ם אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: For from [the] rising of [the] sun and to its setting great [is] my name among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering; for great [is] my name among the nations, says Yahweh of hosts.
pieces: From where the sun rises to where it sets, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name is great among the nations. \q In every place incense is offered to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, and pure offerings, \q because {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name is great among the nations, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

L.11: For from the rising of the sun to its setting great [is] {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name among the nations, \q and in every place incense is brought near to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, and a pure offering; \q for great [is] {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name among the nations, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts.

R.11: From where the sun rises to where it sets, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name is honored among the nations. \q Everywhere people burn incense to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and bring offerings that are pure. \q My name is great among the nations, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

decisions.choice: from the rising of the sun to its setting: from east to west, all over the world
decisions.reason: The phrase means the whole earth (Psalm 50:1; 113:3; Isaiah 45:6). |

decisions.choice: my name is great among the nations: the LORD honored by the nations, now or in time to come
alternatives: my name will be great among the nations
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no verb "is" or "will be", and the offering is described with participles, so the verse may speak of the present or of the future. Read as present, it may mean that the nations, in their own way, honor the God of heaven, or that Jews scattered among the nations worship him; read as future, it is a promise like Zephaniah 2:11 and Isaiah 45:6. Either way it shames the priests of verse 10. From early times Christian writers read it of the church's worship among the nations. The text leaves the time open, and the wording here keeps the Hebrew present.

decisions.choice: incense is offered: offerings burned, as the smoke of incense
decisions.reason: The first word means something made to go up in smoke, usually incense. The offerings brought "in every place" contrast with the defiled offerings in the one temple. |

decisions.choice: is honored (R); burn incense to me (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "honored" for "great" in the first line and keeps "great" in the third, and says "burn incense to me" for "incense is offered to my name", since the name stands for the LORD himself. |

records.source: וְאַתֶּ֖ם מְחַלְּלִ֣ים אוֹת֑וֹ בֶּאֱמָרְכֶ֗ם שֻׁלְחַ֤ן אֲדֹנָי֙ מְגֹאָ֣ל ה֔וּא וְנִיב֖וֹ נִבְזֶ֥ה אָכְלֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: But you [are] profaning it in your saying, [The] table of [the] Lord, it [is] defiled, and its fruit, its food, [is] despicable.
pieces: But you profane it \q by saying, "The Lord's table is defiled, \q and the food on it can be despised."

L.12: But you are profaning it \q in your saying, "The table of the Lord, it is defiled, \q and its fruit, its food, is despicable."

R.12: But you treat {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name as if it were not holy. \q You say, "The Lord's altar is unclean, \q and the food offered on it does not deserve respect."

decisions.choice: profaning it: profaning the LORD's name
decisions.reason: "It" is the name the nations honor (verse 11). To profane is to treat what is holy as common. |

decisions.choice: its fruit, its food: what is offered on the altar
decisions.reason: The first word, "its fruit", is rare and may mean the produce brought to the altar, or the priests' share of it. Some think it is a copying slip, written twice. "Its food" explains it.

decisions.choice: the table of the Lord is defiled: as in verse 7
decisions.reason: The charge of verse 7 is repeated. Here the word for the Lord is Adonai, not the divine name. |

decisions.choice: treat my name as if it were not holy (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "it" refers to and what profaning means (m1). |

records.source: וַאֲמַרְתֶּם֩ הִנֵּ֨ה מַתְּלָאָ֜ה וְהִפַּחְתֶּ֣ם אוֹת֗וֹ אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת וַהֲבֵאתֶ֣ם גָּז֗וּל וְאֶת־הַפִּסֵּ֨חַ֙ וְאֶת־הַ֣חוֹלֶ֔ה וַהֲבֵאתֶ֖ם אֶת־הַמִּנְחָ֑ה הַאֶרְצֶ֥ה אוֹתָ֛הּ מִיֶּדְכֶ֖ם אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And you say, Look, what a weariness! And you sniff at it, says Yahweh of hosts; and you bring [what was] stolen and the lame and the sick, and you bring the offering. Will I accept it from your hand? says Yahweh.
pieces: You say, "What a burden this is!" and you sniff at it in contempt, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies. \q You bring animals that were stolen, or lame or sick, \q and these you bring as your offering! \q Should I accept that from your hands? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.13: And you say, "Look, what a weariness!" and you sniff at it, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts; \q and you bring what was stolen, and the lame and the sick; \q and you bring the offering! \q Shall I accept it from your hand? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.13: You say, "We are so tired of all this!" And you turn up your noses at it, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies. \q You bring animals that were stolen, or lame, or sick, \q and you offer them to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}! \q Should I accept them from you? says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: you sniff at it: you snort at it in contempt
decisions.reason: The verb means to blow or puff. The priests sniff at their duty as at something worthless. |

decisions.choice: at it: at the altar and its service
decisions.reason: Jewish scribal tradition lists this among a few places where the scribes changed a word out of reverence: it says that the original read "you sniff at me" and that "at it" was written instead. The meaning is the same in the end: contempt for the service is contempt for the LORD.

decisions.choice: what was stolen: animals taken by robbery
decisions.reason: The word means taken by force. An animal gained by robbery could not be offered (Leviticus 5:23 in the Hebrew numbering). Some take it as an animal mauled by a wild beast, which also could not be offered (Exodus 22:30).

decisions.choice: animals that were stolen, or lame or sick (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "animals". The priests' words are set in double quotes. |

records.source: וְאָר֣וּר נוֹכֵ֗ל וְיֵ֤שׁ בְּעֶדְרוֹ֙ זָכָ֔ר וְנֹדֵ֛ר וְזֹבֵ֥חַ מָשְׁחָ֖ת לַֽאדֹנָ֑י כִּי֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ גָּד֜וֹל אָ֗נִי אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת וּשְׁמִ֖י נוֹרָ֥א בַגּוֹיִֽם׃
records.gloss: And cursed [is the] cheat, and [there is] in his flock a male, and [he] vows and sacrifices a blemished [one] to [the] Lord; for a great king [am] I, says Yahweh of hosts, and my name [is] feared among the nations.
pieces: Cursed is the cheat who has a sound male in {{gender:their|his}} flock and vows to give it, \q but then sacrifices to the Lord an animal with a blemish! \q I am a great King, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, \q and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name is feared among the nations.

L.14: Cursed is the cheat who has a male in {{gender:their|his}} flock, \q and vows [it], but sacrifices a blemished [animal] to the Lord; \q for a great King [am] I, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, \q and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name is feared among the nations.

R.14: A curse on anyone who cheats like this! They have a good male animal in their flock and promise to give it, \q but then they offer the Lord an animal that has something wrong with it. \q I am a great King, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, \q and the nations fear {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name.

decisions.choice: a male, a vow, a blemished animal: a vow paid with a defective animal
decisions.reason: A vow offering had to be a male without defect (Leviticus 22:18-21). The cheat has a good animal but brings a damaged one, keeping the better for himself. |

decisions.choice: I am a great King: the LORD is King over all nations
decisions.reason: "Great king" was a title of the emperors of Assyria and Persia (2 Kings 18:19). The LORD is the great King over all the earth (Psalm 47:3; 95:3), whose name the nations fear (verse 11). He deserves better than the governor of verse 8. |

decisions.choice: feared: held in awe
decisions.reason: The word means "to be feared", awesome, as in Zephaniah 2:11. |

decisions.choice: the Lord (Adonai); King with a capital K; the gender setting for the cheat
decisions.reason: "Lord" stands for Adonai, as the settled wording for this title of God. "King" is capitalized as a title of God. The cheat may be any owner of a flock, so Literal and Balanced use the gender setting and Readable says "anyone ... they". |
